questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Course options, English-speaking country, good ranking of the University, interest in the country/culture, somewhere I couldn't easily visit otherwise, safety etc.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was definitely an up and down. The beginning was quite harsh (hadn't found my people yet, stressful, bad weather), while the end was amazing (good friends, better weather, not as stressful).

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Students services helped with the registration and settling in. There is also something called Ask Otago, where you can always go to or call for help with basically everything.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I would have wished for more opportunities to connect with the other students, since the different seminars were not really interactive.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Uniflats, colleges or private flats.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Every flat comes with a kitchen (including basic kitchen utensils). There is no meal plan available. Colleges offer that but that is only available for first-year students that stay a whole year as far as I know.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It's the easiest to get into. The quality varies greatly though but at least everyone is somewhat close to their lecture halls. Uniflats also organises a lot of events which is nice.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: While my flat was cheap, I had no idea what it looked like beforehand and was quite negatively surprised when I ended up in a run-down house wit cracks, leaks and spots everywhere. There was also only one small bathroom (for five people) and the fridge space was a joke as well. I also had nothing in common with my flatmates which was really sad. Other people ended up in a very modern flat and became best friends with their housemates so it's really about luck.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very easy.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It's an online process but the steps are ver well described so it's not too difficult to get things right. If in doubt, one could also always contact Ask Otago for help.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Ask Otago (visit in person, mail or call).

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got into all of the courses I wanted to. Since I only did postgrad courses I did have to apply for special permission but that was a really easy process.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just make sure that you pick courses that actually work for you. This means that there are no timetable overlaps and that you're actually eligible for the courses you want to take.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Good lecturers, very small groups (6-9 people) for postgrad courses. Not too difficult. Workload very manageabale.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took one 400-level and two 700-level courses which are all considered postgraduate.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: My courses at the Department of Public Health were very similar to the ones at KU. It was lecture-style, but we could always ask questions and there were small group works every now and then. We also had to read book chapters and listen to podcasts etc. before the class. My course at the Department of Anthropology was a lot more interactive and intimate, building on weekly forum posts and intense discussions, so quite different to KU.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Anth431 People, Culture and Development; Pubh732 Using Epidemiology in Public Health Practice; Pubh736 Economic Evaluation.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Honestly, all of them but keep in mind your previous knowledge and skills. Pubh732 was a little boring since I already knew a lot of the course content from my previous courses during my BA and MA. Pubh736 was the most hands-on and perhaps the most valuable for me in terms of skills and knowledge acquired. Anth431 was amazing because of the teacher and my fellow students, and really helped in gaining a new perspective on international development (aid).

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Maybe medical expenses. I had to visit the urgent doctors once which cost me 90$ (as an exchange student you qualify for the local rate). I could have reclaimed that with my insurance but I didn't find the time to do so and didn't have the motivation to familiarise myself with that process.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries were extremely expensive, especially fresh produce. But prices also varied greatly, when I first arrived, a cucumber would cost 9$, while it was sitting at 3$ by the end of my stay. The bus was fairly cheap with 2.50$ per ride. Eating out is cheaper than in Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Many different options at all prices.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Basically everything, from ski club to jiu jitsu, to tennis and arts and crafts. The gym is free for every student and it also rents out outdoor equipment like surfboards, bikes or tents. There were some events for students (mostly rganised by uniflats) to visit places or socialise. There was also the opportunity to volunteer.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Volunteer and get your Global Impact Scholar Programme certificate. I can highly recommend the Good Deed and Feed as well as the Reading Oasis. I also had a good time at the Tennis Association (we played each Friday). i also joined the Women in Health Network Otago which was really nice for networking.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Surf at St. Clairs, go for hikes (e.g. Highcliff Track), visit the Botanical Gardens and Baldwin Street, go for trips (e.g. Queenstown, Christchurch, Mount Cook, Lake Tekapo, Wanaka, Invercargill etc.). There is so much to see, but you do need a car for most things. The buses only go as far and often only drive once an hour. Also, definitely visit a rugby match.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, not too different from Northern/Western Europe and previous places I've been to.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It is honestly very difficult to make local friends. Most exchange students only really connected with other exchange students. Try to go to house parties and try to befriend people in your class. Other than that, the only option is to join clubs and societies with locals in it or just be super open and talk to everyone.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing really.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The wonderful singing and dancing culture of the Maori. Also, everyone is a lot more open, friendly and laid-back here which can be very nice.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1. Don't have too many expectations since it will be different than what you're imagining it to be. 2. Be open-minded and try to use every opportunity you can to go out and meet up with people. 3. Enjoy your time and don't be afraid to tell people when things are rough and you need some support.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Dunedin is a small and run-down town with an intense party culture. You might feel a little out of place when you're over the age of 20 and not into constantly drinking and partying.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The connections and memories I made along the way.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Probably my flatmates and the housing situation. I'm used to being abroad for months so that was fine for me but I did miss my partner, friends and family back home. The time-zone difference was also rough.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I was very disappointed that I, as an international student at KU, had absolutely no opportunity to connect with the Danish KU students, so I had to come here completely alone, while all the Danish students connected beforehand. That just didn't seem fair and while I understand that I'm not Danish, I still live in Cph and go to the same University as the other students.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
